solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Determined to listen to Edward on strong beer

indicators.note: In an across clue, X on Y puts X after Y.

parts.note: Stout is a dark, strong beer.
To listen to is to hear.
Ted is a short form of Edward.

explanation.surface: Someone is set on hearing out Edward's views about strong beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The order differs from the surface: in an across clue, "on" places the listening and Edward after the beer, not before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stout-hearted is brave and resolute, which is determined.

clue.text: Vehicle taking another one up hill

indicators.note: In a down clue, up means read from the bottom.

parts.note: Another vehicle: a cart.
A tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor.

explanation.surface: One vehicle tows another up a steep hill.
explanation.walkthrough: "Another one" means another vehicle, pointing back to the definition. A tor is a rocky hilltop in the West of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this heavy farm machine is one kind of vehicle, and it hauls loads just as the towing picture in the surface suggests.

clue.text: Before ten, mail unfortunately not dispatched? Tough

indicators.note: before means the unsent piece comes ahead of the rearranged letters

parts.note: a letter not dispatched is unsent

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so the letters of ten and mail are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sadly the post went unsent before ten o'clock; hard luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough' sounds like a sympathetic shrug but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tough is hard-headed and unemotional, unswayed by feelings.

clue.text: Strike by footballer? It tops the page

definitions.meaning: A footballer strikes the ball with the head.
The running line printed along the top of every page of a document.

explanation.surface: A footballer's goal makes the top of the newspaper page.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are a football shot with the head and the running line at the top of a page.
explanation.definitionFit: A header is both a headed shot in football and the text at the top of a page.

clue.text: Liable to slip up with account I had open, rent going astray

parts.note: I had contracts to I'd

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so the letters of open and rent are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone clumsy keeps an account open while the rent goes missing.
explanation.walkthrough: ACC and ID come first, then 'going astray' rearranges OPEN and RENT into ENTPRONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Accident-prone describes a person who has mishaps more often than most.

clue.text: Test of divisions in society — not British

parts.note: Tribal describes divisions of society into tribes.
B is the standard abbreviation for British; it is removed.

explanation.surface: A sociologist tests how society is divided, excluding the British.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIBAL loses its B to leave TRIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a trial is a test of how something performs, as in a clinical trial or a trial run.

clue.text: Waste a long time in underground prison

parts.note: Dung is animal waste.
An eon is an age.

explanation.surface: A prisoner wastes years locked below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: "Waste" looks like a verb in the surface; it is the noun dung.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the dark cell beneath a castle keep where captives were held.

clue.text: Thin gooey stuff, almost

indicators.note: Almost means not quite complete, so the last letter goes.

parts.note: Slime is gooey stuff; its last letter is dropped.

explanation.surface: Something runny and gooey is nearly too thin.
explanation.walkthrough: "Thin" and "gooey" seem to describe the same liquid; thin is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe a slender figure, and both can also mean small, as in a slim or thin chance.

clue.text: Lots of young men around ring

indicators.note: Around means encircling, so the young men encircle the ring.

parts.note: Lads are young men.
O is ring-shaped.

explanation.surface: Lots of young men gather round a boxing ring.
explanation.walkthrough: O stands for a ring because of its shape.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: both are casual ways of saying a great many, as in loads of time.

clue.text: A disturbance when not starting sale

indicators.note: not starting means the first letter is dropped from the word for disturbance

parts.note: a ruction is a noisy disturbance or row

explanation.surface: A commotion breaks out when the sale fails to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: A is followed by RUCTION with 'not starting' removing its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An auction is a public sale where goods go to the highest bidder.

clue.text: Friend comes around in time finally for early show

indicators.note: comes around means the friend's letters are wrapped around the rest

parts.note: a mate is a friend

indicators.note: finally means only the last letter of time is used

parts.note: last letter of time

explanation.surface: A friend visits just in time for an early showing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is used as written, a piece of the wordplay rather than a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinee is an afternoon performance, given earlier than the usual evening show.

clue.text: Some wood elves do a lot of digging

indicators.note: Some of the letters of wood elves give the answer.

parts.note: The last letter of wood plus the first four of elves.

explanation.surface: Some woodland elves spend their time digging.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the gap between wood and elves.
explanation.definitionFit: To delve is to dig, or to search deeply.

clue.text: Street rodent seen round one narrow passage

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street.

indicators.note: Seen round means placed on both sides of, so the rodent surrounds the one.

parts.note: A rat is a rodent.
I is one as a Roman numeral.

explanation.surface: A rat is spotted in a street near a narrow alley.
explanation.walkthrough: The narrow passage is a sea channel, not an alleyway.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait is a narrow passage of water between two seas.

clue.text: Singer of rap soon out of order

indicators.note: Out of order means not in the right sequence, so the letters are rearranged.

parts.note: RAP SOON rearranged.

explanation.surface: A singer's rap will soon be judged out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: "Out of order" reads as unacceptable in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this is one kind of singer, the highest female or boy's voice in a choir.

clue.text: Bury an indefinite number put in prison

parts.note: To inter is to bury.
In maths, n stands for an unspecified number.

explanation.surface: A number of people are buried or locked away.
explanation.walkthrough: n is used in maths for an unspecified number.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern is to confine someone, especially in wartime.

clue.text: Variable beer served up with a lot of abuse

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: a lot of means most of the word, so its last letter is cut

parts.note: stick is informal British for criticism or abuse

explanation.surface: Beer of changing strength was dished out alongside plenty of insults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' turns ALE into ELA; 'a lot of' trims STICK to STIC. Giving someone stick is British slang for mocking them.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic describes something flexible or adaptable, such as an elastic schedule that can vary.

clue.text: Tries to have little time in suit

indicators.note: To have something is to hold it, so the word for tries holds the little time inside.

parts.note: A judge hears, that is tries, a case.
T is the abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: Someone tries to find a little time for a legal suit.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tries" and "suit" point to the courtroom, but the suit is one of the four in a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts is one of the four suits in cards.

clue.text: Fool cutting exercise out?

indicators.note: Cutting means slicing into, so the fool slices into the middle of the exercise.

parts.note: PE is physical education.
An ass is a fool.

explanation.surface: A fool skips the exercise class.
explanation.walkthrough: "Out" means out of fashion; "cutting exercise out" reads as dropping it.
explanation.definitionFit: Passé means out of date, out of fashion.

clue.text: What will help one see small particles on the air

indicators.note: Broadcast words are heard, not read, so the answer only sounds like the wordplay.

parts.note: Specks are tiny particles.

explanation.surface: Something to help one see dust floating in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: "On the air" seems to describe where the dust floats.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the answer is informal for spectacles, and glasses are exactly what will help one see.

clue.text: Account for cross appearing in strange alpine

indicators.note: appearing in means the cross shows up inside the other letters
strange means odd, so the letters of alpine are rearranged

parts.note: X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: A cross turns up somewhere odd in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges ALPINE as EPLAIN, and 'appearing in' sets X inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To explain something is to give the reasons for it, which is to account for it.

clue.text: Number taken from sixty

definitions.meaning: The surface reading is a subtraction sum; the meant reading is a numeral lifted out of a word.
Take letters from the word itself: its middle two form a Roman numeral.

explanation.surface: A number subtracted from sixty.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters IX sit inside sIXty, and IX is the Roman numeral for nine, which the grid wants written out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the number: Roman IX is literally taken from the middle of the word sixty.

clue.text: A more acceptable helper

parts.note: Used as it stands.
Better means more acceptable.

explanation.surface: One assistant is preferable to another.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as A BETTER.
explanation.definitionFit: An abetter is someone who helps, usually in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Frequently melt missing shillings

parts.note: To soften is to melt, as butter does.
S is the abbreviation for shillings, an old British coin; it is removed.

explanation.surface: Snow often melts, costing shillings.
explanation.walkthrough: A shilling was a pre-decimal British coin, abbreviated s.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean many times over, as in he often or frequently visits.

clue.text: Close obscene broadcasting, offering redundancy

indicators.note: Broadcasting scatters things widely, so the letters are scattered.

parts.note: CLOSE OBSCENE rearranged.

explanation.surface: A regulator closes an obscene channel, leaving its staff redundant.
explanation.walkthrough: "Broadcasting" belongs with the TV picture, but here it scatters the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsolescence is the state of being no longer needed, redundancy.
